# Results — Study 399 (Kalshi-Efficiency)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Are Kalshi event-contract prices
**well-calibrated**, or is there a free edge in the mispricing? Kalshi's resolved-contract
history is **not free**, so this is a **methods demo on a transparent, clearly-labelled
illustrative book** of binary event-contracts — NOT a backtest of live Kalshi prices. Each
contract has a market price `p` (the crowd's implied probability) and a realized binary
`outcome`; calibration asks whether YES occurred about `p` of the time. The illustrative tape
carries a mild **favourite–longshot bias** (longshots over-priced, favourites under-priced) so
the calibration curve has something to show. Offline & deterministic; run `python
examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| "Real" tape | **ILLUSTRATIVE** seeded book of resolved binary event-contracts (NOT live Kalshi — Kalshi history isn't free) |
| Contracts | **4,000** binaries; price ∈ [0.02, 0.98]; YES base rate **50.3%** |
| As-of | 2026-06-22 (cache built deterministically; no future stamp) |
| Baked bias | favourite–longshot tilt **edge = 0.04** (a transparent illustration, named everywhere) |
| Strategy | long favourites (price ≥ 0.80) + short longshots (price ≤ 0.20); **1-cent one-way fee per leg** |
| Inference | Brier reliability term (Murphy 1973), Welch *t* of net P&L vs 0, 20,000-draw within-bucket randomization null |

> **Illustration caveat (named on the Signal axis).** The "real" tape here is a **constructed
> illustration**, not a measurement of live Kalshi prices. Its significance is *planted by
> construction* (we put a 4-cent favourite–longshot bias in), so it can never back a `REAL`
> Signal stamp — that bar needs a robust *t* ≥ 2 on a **real tape**, which is not available
> for free. The study's job is to show the *machinery* (calibration curve, Brier decomposition,
> spread + randomization null, fee) and what it does to a finite book — a methods demo in the
> spirit of [Study 351](../351-btc-5m-polymarket-momentum/) and the research-method demos 343–350.

## The calibration curve — does YES occur as often as priced?

Realized YES frequency per price decile, against the bucket's mean price (the diagonal is
perfect calibration). The illustrative tape bows the classic favourite–longshot way.

| price bucket | mean price | realized YES freq | n | gap (freq − price) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0–0.1 | 0.059 | **0.035** | 257 | **−0.024** (longshot over-priced) |
| 0.1–0.2 | 0.149 | 0.090 | 354 | −0.058 |
| 0.4–0.5 | 0.452 | 0.431 | 501 | −0.021 |
| 0.5–0.6 | 0.551 | 0.554 | 498 | +0.003 (≈ fair near 0.5) |
| 0.8–0.9 | 0.847 | 0.868 | 400 | +0.020 |
| 0.9–1.0 | 0.937 | **0.972** | 254 | **+0.035** (favourite under-priced) |

Longshots resolve YES **less** often than priced; favourites **more** often — the racetrack
distortion. The Brier reliability (mis-calibration) term is **0.00086** — small, because the
bias is mild and a finite book is noisy.

## The harvestable spread — and what the fee does to it

Going long favourites and short longshots, per-contract net P&L (in cents), with a 1-cent
one-way fee per leg. The win-rate is high **because favourites win often** — a base-rate
number, not an edge.

| fee / leg | n trades | gross mean | net mean | win-rate | Welch *t* | randomization *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0¢ | 1,265 | **+3.45¢** | +3.45¢ | 92% | 4.60 | 0.000 |
| **1.0¢** (illustrative) | 1,265 | +3.45¢ | **+2.45¢** | 92% | **3.26** | 0.000 |
| 2.0¢ | 1,265 | +3.45¢ | +1.45¢ | 90% | 1.93 | 0.000 |
| 3.0¢ | 1,265 | +3.45¢ | **+0.45¢** | 85% | **0.60** | 0.000 |

Read it carefully. Even with a **planted** 4-cent bias, the gross spread is only ~3.5¢, and a
**1-cent** fee already eats a third of it. At a realistic **2–3¢** round of fee + bid/ask the
*t* collapses through the t ≥ 2 bar to **0.60** — the harvestable edge is gone. This is the
whole tradability story: the mispricing that the literature documents is **a few cents**, and
an exchange's fee and the bid/ask sit exactly on top of it. The cheap longshot/rich favourite
you screen for isn't the price you trade (cf. Study 351).

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, and `edge=0` stays quiet

On a deterministic book where we **know** the truth: `edge=0` must be perfectly calibrated and
must **not** manufacture a tradable spread; a large planted edge must light up.

| planted edge | reliability ×10⁴ | n | gross mean | net mean | win-rate | Welch *t* | randomization *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (calibrated) | 1.83 | 1,201 | −0.48¢ | **−1.48¢** | 88% | **−1.59** | 0.708 |
| **0.08** (large bias) | 45.22 | 1,201 | +6.77¢ | **+5.77¢** | 95% | **9.47** | 0.000 |

With **no** bias the calibration error is ~0, the net spread is **negative** (the fee on a
fair book is a pure cost), and the test does **not** fire (*t* = −1.59, *p* = 0.71) — even
though the raw win-rate is still **88%** (favourites win; that is the base rate, not an edge).
A large planted bias inflates the reliability term **25×** and drives *t* to 9.5. The control
proves two things at once: the measurement engine is unbiased, **and** a high win-rate alone
never implies an edge — only a calibration *gap* net of the fee does.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** This is a **methods demo on an illustrative book**, not a measurement of
  live Kalshi. The significance on the illustrative tape is *planted by construction* and can
  never back a `REAL` stamp (which needs a robust *t* ≥ 2 on a **real tape** — not free for
  Kalshi). The calibration machinery is validated by the synthetic control; **no real,
  harvestable mispricing is claimed.**
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Even a *planted* 4-cent favourite–longshot bias nets only ~2.4¢
  after a 1-cent fee, and a realistic **2–3¢** fee + bid/ask takes the *t* below 2 (to 0.60).
  EV per binary share is `outcome − price − fee`; the documented few-cent mispricing is
  exactly the size the exchange's costs eat. No NAV-scale edge survives.
- **Free edge in the mispricing? — BUSTED.** The favourite–longshot bias is real in the
  literature, but the *harvestable* part lives **inside** the fee and the spread. The 92%
  win-rate that makes the pitch glow is base rate × the fact that favourites win — the same
  high-confidence/no-edge shape as [Study 351](../351-btc-5m-polymarket-momentum/).
